Exact lines
scope: Dan asked (3 Nov) for whatever is most relevant to the January course. GCSE physics topics his app does not yet teach are waves and atomic physics; everything else (forces, motion, momentum, moments, energy, power, pressure, heat, gases, electricity, magnetism) is built. So this course fills those two gaps and ends with exam-style practice. Seven lessons in about this order (the brief may merge or split): (1) Waves: what a wave carries (energy, not matter), transverse and longitudinal, amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period T = 1/f, and v = f lambda. (2) Sound and sonar: sound as a longitudinal wave, its speed in air, water and steel, hearing range and ultrasound, echo timing (distance = speed x time / 2) for depth sounding and sonar, general physics only. (3) The electromagnetic spectrum: the families from radio to gamma in order, all at the speed of light in a vacuum, v = f lambda with c, what each is used for and its hazards, which are ionising. (4) Atoms and isotopes: protons, neutrons and electrons, sizes, nuclear notation (mass and atomic numbers), isotopes and ions, a brief model history only where it helps. (5) Radioactive decay: alpha, beta and gamma (what each is, how far it goes, what stops it, how ionising), balancing decay equations, irradiation versus contamination. (6) Half-life: random decay, activity in becquerels, reading half-life from a graph or count table, how much is left after n half-lives, background radiation and dose in sieverts at GCSE level. (7) Mixed practice: GCSE-style puzzles across all of physics, equations recalled not given, units beside the box (forces and motion, moments, momentum, energy and power and efficiency, pressure and density, specific heat and latent heat, electricity, waves, radioactivity), as a final check before January; a typed answer for every figure. Each lesson opens with a puzzle he can feel his way through, then the rule, then typed-answer puzzles he works on paper. Nuclear fission, chain reactions and reactors are out: they belong to his Navy course, so mention at most that they come later. Examples from engineering and the sea where they fit (echo sounding, sonar in general, radio, infrared cameras for hot joints, non-destructive testing with ultrasound or gamma); never claim how the Navy or a boat does it
later: Waves and light (Science shelf, Physics folder: interference, the Doppler effect and the nature of light; this course takes waves only to GCSE)
